output.title: Second opinions should be a gate, not a guess
output.body:
If you want AI in a small business workflow, treat second opinions as a design rule, not a vibe. The question is simple: when should the system stop and ask for a human decision instead of acting on its own?

Use one concrete boundary. For money movement and other high-risk decisions, human approval is mandatory. For routine work like data entry, customer replies, or document classification, you can define a review rule later in the pilot: if the system is uncertain, it flags the item for review instead of pushing it through. That keeps the owner in charge of the final call.

The practical test is this: which decision in your workflow would cost you more to reverse than to pause for five minutes? Write those down first. That gives you the gate. Everything outside it can stay manual, or be handled with a lighter check. No need to make AI the office hall monitor.

One useful next step is to map a single recurring workflow and mark each decision as “human only,” “AI can suggest,” or “AI can act.” Bareni’s working approach is to start with that one workflow, confirm whether AI fits at all, and define scope, measures, and account ownership in the customer’s name from the start. Finished code is handed over; the control stays with the owner.
